## Introduction

I use Netflix's seven viewing reports to compare hours watched and suggest what to invest in for 2027.

## Task 1: Load the data

I use the loading code provided in the assignment.

```{r}
#' Acquire Netflix What We Watched Reports
#' 
#' This function will acquire and standardize all data for MP#01
#' from Netflix. Because Netflix hosts the data files behind a CDN, we
#' are accessing the release pages and automatically extracting links to the
#' relevant files (with CDN hash). 
#' 
#' After import, files are stacked vertically and some basic cleaning is
#' performed. 
load_netflix_data <- function(){
  # Note to students: Make sure you have installed the tidyverse and fs packages
  #                   before beginning this assignment. If you aren't sure,
  #                   simply run `library(tidyverse)` at your R Console and, if
  #                   you don't see an error message, `tidyverse` has been 
  #                   installed. (Same for `fs`) If you still need to install
  #                   either package, use the `install.packages` function as 
  #                   demonstrated in class.
  library(tidyverse)
  library(rvest)
  library(readxl)
  library(fs)
  
  data_dir <- path("data", "mp01")
    
  if(!dir_exists(data_dir)){
    dir_create(data_dir, showWarnings=FALSE, recurse=TRUE)
  }
  
  NETFLIX_URLS <- list(
    `2023H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-a-netflix-engagement-report",
    `2023H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2023",
    `2024H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2024",
    `2024H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2024",
    `2025H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2025",
    `2025H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2025",
    `2026H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2026"
  )
  
  download_if_needed <- function(url, local){
    if(!file_exists(local)){
      download.file(url, local, quiet = TRUE, mode = "wb")
    }
    
    return(local)
  }
    
  NETFLIX_URLS |> 
    map(read_html) |> 
    map(html_element, xpath = "//a[contains(@href, '.xlsx')]") |> 
    map_chr(html_attr, "href") |> 
    enframe("period", "url") |> 
   mutate(path = path(data_dir, paste0(period, ".xlsx")), 
          path = map2(url, path, download_if_needed), 
          data = map(path, read_excel, skip=3, na="*"), 
          data = map(data, \(x) x |> mutate(`Release Date` = as.Date(`Release Date`)))) |>
    unnest(data) |> 
    select(-url, -path) |> 
    mutate(year=str_sub(period, 1, 4), 
           half=str_sub(period, start=6), 
           period_start = make_date(year, if_else(half==1, 1, 7), 1), 
           period_end = make_date(year, if_else(half==1, 6, 12), if_else(half==1, 30, 31))) |> 
    filter(!is.na(`Hours Viewed`)) |> 
    mutate(live_event = !is.na(Runtime) & str_detect(Runtime, "\\d+:\\d+\\*"), 
           clean_time = str_remove(Runtime, fixed("*")),
           Runtime = 60 * hour(hm(clean_time)) + minute(hm(clean_time))) |>
    select(-clean_time) |>
    mutate(Runtime = coalesce(Runtime, mean(Runtime, na.rm=TRUE)), 
           .by=Title, 
           Title = stringi::stri_trans_general(Title, "Latin-ASCII"),
           Title = str_remove(Title, " // .*"), 
           Title = str_remove(Title, "[^[:ascii:]].*"), 
           Title = str_trim(Title)) |>
    filter_out(Title == "") |>
    select(year, 
           period, 
           period_start, 
           period_end, 
           Title, 
           -half, 
           Runtime, 
           Views, 
           `Hours Viewed`, 
           `Release Date`,
           `Available Globally?`, 
           live_event)
}

NETFLIX_DATA <- load_netflix_data()
```

## Task 2: Fix column names

I use lowercase names with underscores instead of spaces.

```{r}
NETFLIX_DATA <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  rename(title = Title, runtime = Runtime, views = Views,
         hours_viewed = `Hours Viewed`, release_date = `Release Date`,
         available_globally = `Available Globally?`)
```

## Task 3: Fix column types

I convert year to an integer and global availability to TRUE/FALSE.

```{r}
NETFLIX_DATA <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  mutate(year = as.integer(year),
         available_globally = available_globally == "Yes")

library(gt)
library(scales)
```

## Task 4: Initial data checks

```{r}
glimpse(NETFLIX_DATA)
summary(NETFLIX_DATA)
```

```{r}
checks <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  summarise(rows = n(), missing_runtime = sum(is.na(runtime)),
            missing_release = sum(is.na(release_date)),
            missing_views = sum(is.na(views)),
            mean_hours = mean(hours_viewed), median_hours = median(hours_viewed))
```

There are `r comma(checks$rows)` rows and `r ncol(NETFLIX_DATA)` columns. Each row is one title in a six-month period.

There are `r comma(checks$missing_runtime)` missing runtimes, `r comma(checks$missing_release)` missing release dates, and `r comma(checks$missing_views)` missing view counts. I skip missing runtimes in totals.

Average viewing is `r comma(checks$mean_hours, accuracy = 1)` hours per row, versus a median of `r comma(checks$median_hours)`. A few big titles pull the average up.

## Task 5: Basic viewing patterns

### 1. What dates does the data cover?

```{r}
coverage <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  summarise(start = min(period_start), end = max(period_end))
```

The reports cover **`r format(coverage$start, '%B %d, %Y')` through `r format(coverage$end, '%B %d, %Y')`**.

### 2. How many different shows and movies are included?

```{r}
title_count <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  summarise(titles = n_distinct(title))
```

There are **`r comma(title_count$titles)` different titles**, counting seasons separately.

### 3. How many hours were spent watching the Bridgerton universe?

```{r}
bridgerton <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(str_detect(title, "Bridgerton")) |>
  summarise(hours = sum(hours_viewed))
```

The **Bridgerton universe**, including *Queen Charlotte*, had **`r comma(bridgerton$hours)` hours** watched.

### 4. How many hours were spent watching the five Stranger Things seasons?

```{r}
stranger_things <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(str_detect(title, "Stranger Things")) |>
  filter_out(str_detect(title, "Beyond Stranger Things")) |>
  filter_out(str_detect(title, "Tales from")) |>
  filter_out(str_detect(title, "Fireplace")) |>
  summarise(hours = sum(hours_viewed))
```

The five main **Stranger Things** seasons had **`r comma(stranger_things$hours)` hours** watched, excluding the three companion programs.

### 5. What share of 2026H1 watch time went to the top ten titles?

```{r}
latest <- NETFLIX_DATA |> filter(period == "2026H1")

top10 <- latest |>
  slice_max(hours_viewed, n = 10, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  summarise(share = sum(hours_viewed) / sum(latest$hours_viewed))
```

The **top ten titles in 2026H1** accounted for **`r percent(top10$share, accuracy = 0.1)`** of that period's total viewing hours.

### 6. What fraction of the catalog is globally available?

```{r}
# Use one period to avoid counting titles repeatedly.
global_titles <- latest |>
  filter(available_globally == TRUE)

global <- latest |>
  summarise(titles = n_distinct(global_titles$title) / n_distinct(title),
            hours = sum(global_titles$hours_viewed) / sum(hours_viewed),
            unknown = sum(is.na(available_globally)))
```

For **2026H1**, globally available titles were **`r percent(global$titles, accuracy = 0.1)`** of titles and **`r percent(global$hours, accuracy = 0.1)`** of watch time.
## Task 6: Comparisons

### 1. What was the top title in each period and its viewing share?

```{r}
leaders <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  group_by(period) |>
  mutate(share = hours_viewed / sum(hours_viewed)) |>
  slice_max(hours_viewed, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(period, title, hours_viewed, share)

leaders |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(title = "Most-watched title in each period") |>
  cols_label(period = "Period", title = "Title",
             hours_viewed = "Hours viewed", share = "Share of viewing") |>
  fmt_number(hours_viewed, decimals = 0) |>
  fmt_percent(share, decimals = 1)
```

I ranked titles by hours watched and divided each leader's hours by the period's total.

### 2. How did catalog size and total runtime change?

```{r}
catalog <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  group_by(period) |>
  summarise(titles = n_distinct(title),
            runtime_hours = sum(runtime, na.rm = TRUE) / 60,
            missing_runtime = sum(is.na(runtime)), .groups = "drop")

catalog |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(title = "Size of the reported catalog") |>
  cols_label(period = "Period", titles = "Titles",
             runtime_hours = "Runtime (hours)",
             missing_runtime = "Missing runtimes") |>
  fmt_number(c(titles, runtime_hours, missing_runtime), decimals = 0)
```

Reported titles went from `r comma(first(catalog$titles))` to `r comma(last(catalog$titles))` between `r first(catalog$period)` and `r last(catalog$period)`. Known runtime went from `r comma(first(catalog$runtime_hours), accuracy = 1)` to `r comma(last(catalog$runtime_hours), accuracy = 1)` hours.

### 3. Which titles had consistently high viewing?

I rank titles present in all seven periods by their lowest viewing total. A high minimum means they stayed popular even in their weakest period.

```{r}
staples <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  group_by(title, period) |>
  summarise(hours = sum(hours_viewed), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(title) |>
  summarise(periods = n(), average = mean(hours),
            minimum = min(hours), variation = sd(hours), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(periods == n_distinct(NETFLIX_DATA$period)) |>
  slice_max(minimum, n = 5, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  select(-periods)

staples |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(title = "Five titles with consistently high viewing") |>
  cols_label(title = "Title", average = "Average hours",
             minimum = "Minimum hours", variation = "Standard deviation") |>
  fmt_number(c(average, minimum, variation), decimals = 0)
```

*`r staples$title[1]`* leads, with at least `r comma(staples$minimum[1])` hours every period.

### 4. What share of watch time went to shows versus movies?

I count titles over four hours or with “Season,” “Series,” or “Volume” as shows. The rest are movies, or unknown if runtime is missing.

```{r}
classified <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  mutate(type = case_when(
    str_detect(title, regex("season|series|volume", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "Show",
    runtime > 240 ~ "Show",
    is.na(runtime) ~ "Unknown",
    TRUE ~ "Movie"
  ))

type_shares <- classified |>
  group_by(period, type) |>
  summarise(hours = sum(hours_viewed), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(period) |>
  mutate(share = hours / sum(hours)) |>
  ungroup()

type_shares |>
  select(period, type, share) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = type, values_from = share, values_fill = 0) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(title = "Share of viewing by estimated content type") |>
  cols_label(period = "Period") |>
  fmt_percent(where(is.numeric), decimals = 1)
```

These are shares of watch time, including unknown titles in the total, not shares of viewers.

### 5. How did live events compare with recorded content?

I compare average hours and the top entry for each group, using only periods with marked live events. One entry is a title in one period.

```{r}
live_periods <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(live_event) |>
  distinct(period) |>
  pull(period)

live_comparison <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(period %in% live_periods) |>
  mutate(content = if_else(live_event, "Live", "Recorded")) |>
  group_by(content) |>
  summarise(entries = n(), average = mean(hours_viewed),
            top_tier = max(hours_viewed), .groups = "drop")

live_comparison |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(title = "Live and recorded content",
             subtitle = "Hours per title per reporting period") |>
  cols_label(content = "Content", entries = "Entries",
             average = "Average hours", top_tier = "Top entry hours") |>
  fmt_number(c(entries, average, top_tier), decimals = 0)

live <- live_comparison |> filter(content == "Live")
recorded <- live_comparison |> filter(content == "Recorded")
```

Live averaged **`r ifelse(live$average > recorded$average, 'more', 'fewer')` hours**: `r comma(live$average, accuracy = 1)` versus `r comma(recorded$average, accuracy = 1)` for recorded content. The top live entry had `r comma(live$top_tier, accuracy = 1)` hours versus `r comma(recorded$top_tier, accuracy = 1)` for the top recorded entry.

## Supporting R for the memo

```{r}
show_trend <- type_shares |>
  filter(type == "Show") |>
  arrange(period)

global_trend <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  group_by(period) |>
  summarise(share = sum(hours_viewed[available_globally %in% TRUE]) /
              sum(hours_viewed), .groups = "drop")
```

## Task 7: Corporate strategy memo / Op-Ed

**To:** Netflix leadership  
**From:** Christopher Orellana  
**Subject:** Content priorities for 2027

For 2027, I would invest in shows people keep watching and keep a mix of big and smaller titles.

**Keep investing in shows.** The estimated show share went from `r percent(first(show_trend$share), accuracy = 0.1)` of watch time in `r first(show_trend$period)` to `r percent(last(show_trend$share), accuracy = 0.1)` in `r last(show_trend$period)`. I would keep shows a large part of the budget while still making movies.

**Keep older and smaller titles too.** The top ten titles made up only `r percent(top10$share, accuracy = 0.1)` of 2026H1 viewing. *`r staples$title[1]`* had at least `r comma(staples$minimum[1])` hours every half-year. Netflix should keep titles with steady demand instead of focusing only on new hits.

**Think about global audiences.** Globally available titles were `r percent(global$titles, accuracy = 0.1)` of the 2026H1 catalog and earned `r percent(global$hours, accuracy = 0.1)` of watch time. I would fund some original projects that appeal across countries while keeping regional content.

Before setting the budget, Netflix should check costs and whether titles help keep subscribers. Watch time alone does not show profit.
